projects.title: BantAI Elderly Monitoring System
projects.outcome: Defended Capstone : 96.8% of falls caught, families alerted in 20s, no cameras & wearables
projects.desc: An IoT system that watches older adults with contactless radar sensors and alerts caregivers on the web and families on their phones.

case.summary: Older adults at home or in care facilities can fall and stay unattended, and most tools give caregivers raw data, not next steps. I built BantAI with two teammates: radar sensors, a cloud backend, AI guidance, and web and mobile apps. It caught 30 of 31 test falls. Demo access on request.

problem: Older adults who live alone or in care facilities can fall and stay unattended, because caregivers and family members cannot watch them at all times. Checks are usually manual, through visits and phone calls, and most monitoring tools give non-clinical caregivers raw data instead of clear next steps.

Wearables depend on the person remembering to wear and charge them, and cameras raise privacy concerns. The system also had to stay non-clinical: it can tell people to check on someone, but it must never diagnose.
solution: BantAI uses two Seeed Studio 60 GHz mmWave radar sensors that detect falls, presence, heart rate and breathing without capturing images. Each sensor sends a reading every five seconds over HTTPS to a Spring Boot backend on Railway. When a fall is found, the backend raises an alert, asks Google Gemini for short non-clinical guidance (with a fixed template if the AI does not answer within 10 seconds), and sends a push notification. Facility caregivers use a React web app and family members use a React Native Android app, both on the same backend.

My parts: the backend (REST API, sign-in and role-based access, the rule engine, AI guidance, push notifications and cloud deployment), the React web app, the firmware for both sensor boards, and most of the mobile app. Edgar Paul Darryl Ingente helped with the web design and the backend, and John Allen Seares redesigned the mobile app's interface.

process.title: Requirements
process.text: We interviewed three people involved in elderly care and reviewed existing monitoring tools, then set eight functional and eight non-functional requirements.

process.title: Design
process.text: The team designed eight screens as a Figma prototype and modeled the system with UML use case, architecture, activity, deployment and ER diagrams.

process.title: Short build cycles
process.text: Each task had its own branch and pull request: 276 commits and 98 merged pull requests across four repositories. A simulator let us build before the sensors arrived.

process.title: Changes from testing
process.text:
User testing and our adviser led to shared-room sensors, setup from a phone, a move to the cloud so families get alerts anywhere, and approval of new facilities.
```

process.title: Testing and evaluation
process.text: We ran 70 black-box test cases with three testers, 111 fall and everyday-movement trials, and an ISO/IEC 25010 evaluation with 13 respondents.

changed: In 111 trials, BantAI raised an alert in 30 of 31 acted falls (96.8%), with a median of 20 seconds from the floor to the phone, and in only 5 of 80 everyday movements (6.3%), mostly while lying on a low sofa near the 0.5 m fall line. Families now get alerts on any network instead of only the facility Wi-Fi, and moving the servers to Singapore cut the response time from the Philippines from about 430 ms to about 222 ms. Thirteen respondents (seven healthcare professionals, four IT experts or students, a family member and a UX researcher) rated the system 4.26 out of 5 on ISO/IEC 25010, highest for functional suitability (4.43) and security (4.35).
next: The System Usability Scale score was 53.08, below the usual benchmark of 68, so first-time users found BantAI hard to learn. I would start there, using the UX researcher's list of fixes and testing with caregivers again. I would also add the option to rewrite the AI guidance on the mobile app, the only black-box case that failed, and work on false alerts near low furniture and on the breathing rate, which read about 3.6 breaths per minute high. Finally, I would run the five sensor checks we skipped and test the system for several months in a real care facility.
